A Path to YOU: Rikki

Where you come from, told through your family tree: who your ancestors were, where they lived, what was written about them, and how much of it we can really be sure of.

Where this comes from

This page is about your ancestors: your parents, their parents, and so on back through the centuries. Almost all of it comes from FamilySearch, a free family-history website where millions of people have worked together on one shared family tree.

In September 2026 a copy was made of everyone that shared tree lists as your ancestors, going back about thirty generations, which is roughly nine hundred years. For each person the copy holds a name, a year of birth and a year of death where they are known, and who their parents were. That copy is the backbone of every chart on this page.

A shared tree is a wonderful starting point, but it isn’t proof. Anyone can add to it, people copy from one another, and old dates are often estimates. So this page also checks the tree against other sources: old newspapers put online by the Library of Congress, old books scanned by the Internet Archive, WikiTree (another shared family tree, where entries are expected to cite their sources) and Wikipedia. Throughout, it tells you how sure each piece is.

One thing to know before you start: both sides of your tree are large, and far back they overlap. Above your father, Jeffrey Boyle, 3,717 people are recorded, and 3,667 of them come through his grandmother Catherine Edna Straley. Above your mother, Diana Thompson, 5,437 are recorded, and 5,362 of them come through her grandfather John Porter Wigness. The biggest gap is your mother’s father’s family: her father, Kenneth Thompson, is recorded, and so are his parents, Thomas and Gladys Thompson, but nothing about who their parents were, not even Gladys’s maiden name. And 718 people appear on both sides of your tree at once. All of those with a recorded birth year were born between the 800s and the 1180s, and both of your parents’ families reach them through the noble families of medieval Europe. One of the closest is Agnes von Zähringen, born in 1155 by the tree’s reckoning, more than twenty generations back on each side. That isn’t unusual: as the section on kings explains, almost anyone with European roots is related this distantly to almost anyone else.

Nobody living is described on this page except you, by your name and the year you were born. Your parents are living too: they are named, with the year each of them was born, and nothing else about them is shown.

Your whole tree in one picture

You are the small circle in the middle. Each ring around you is one generation further back: first your two parents, then your four grandparents, then your eight great-grandparents, doubling every time. Your father’s ancestors fill the left half of the circle and your mother’s the right. Every person recorded in your tree is drawn as a small curved block in the place where they belong.

    More about the picture

    Why do the outer rings look like thin spokes? The circle can only be divided so finely. Past eleven generations, everyone further back is drawn inside the narrow slice of the ancestor they descend from, so long, well-researched family lines appear as spokes.

    What is the pedigree number in the card? Family historians number a pedigree the same way everywhere: you are 1, your father 2, your mother 3, and from there every father is twice their child’s number and every mother one more than that. The card gives that number for anyone who fills a single place in your tree. People who can be reached by several routes have several numbers, so the card leaves it out for them.

    Each bar is one generation back from you: your parents, your grandparents, and so on. Its height is how many people the tree first records at that distance. Because the same person can be reached by many routes, everyone is counted once, at the nearest generation they appear in.

    What this can’t tell you

    Only people with a birth year in the tree can be drawn, and a bar can only end where a death was recorded. Where no death is recorded, the line is dotted and stops short: that isn’t when the person died. The tree holds years rather than exact days, so every bar can be a year out at either end, and an ancestor who outlived your birth but whose death was never written down won’t show as overlapping your life.

          What this can’t tell you

          This is not a route through anyone’s life. Each line is one moment a record puts somebody somewhere, and the gaps between them are years nobody wrote down. A date in quotation marks is the record’s own wording, such as “about” or “before”.

          Names that moved

          Spellings that changed from parent to child

          A surname was written down by whoever kept the record: a clerk, a priest, a census taker. These are the places in your tree where a child’s surname is spelled differently from the father’s. Some are real changes a family made, often on arriving in America; others are only two people typing the same name differently into the shared tree.

              Where the lines stop

                What this can’t tell you

                A wall is where this copy of the tree stops, not where your family stops. Somebody may have researched the next generation without it reaching the shared tree, or the records may sit unread in an archive. An empty place in the pedigree never means nobody was there: everyone has two parents, whether or not they were written down.

                The two sides, side by side

                MeasureYour father’s sideYour mother’s side

                Found in old newspapers and books

                These were found by searching collections of old newspapers and books that have been scanned and put online. A result was kept only when the name, the place and the time all fit. When a match is likely but not certain, it says so. Some entries are stories about the famous people at the far end of your tree, often written down centuries after they lived; those are marked as legend where historians have doubts.

                  One life, told from the records: David Hone

                    What this can’t tell you

                    Most of this timeline comes from one book, William Folsom’s “Fifty Years in the Northwest”, published in 1888, and much of that from a statement David Hone gave the author. A person’s own account is good evidence of what they said about their life, but it isn’t independent proof. The entries that match only on name, place and time are marked with a hollow dot.

                    Family habits

                    Dates in a family tree can tell us about everyday life: how old people were when they had children, how far apart in age husbands and wives were, and how children were named. For these questions the page uses only ancestors born in 1500 or later, and only birth years that don’t end in 0 or 5, because a year ending in 0 or 5 is often somebody’s rough guess.

                    How old parents were when a child was born

                    The bars count how many parents were each age when one of their children was born. The coloured line marks the typical age: half the parents were younger, and half were older.

                    In northwestern Europe, including Norway, the German lands, Britain and Ireland, people usually married late compared with many other parts of the world. Women often married in their mid-twenties and went on having children into their forties. That is why the typical mother’s age here may be higher than you expect: it counts every child a woman had, not just her first.

                    How far apart husbands and wives were in age

                    Children named for a grandparent

                      Naming customs varied from place to place. In rural Norway there was a strong custom: the first son was named after his father’s father, and the first daughter after her father’s mother, and the next son and daughter usually after the mother’s parents. In German-speaking villages a child was very often named after a godparent, and so many boys were baptised Johann or Hans that they often went by their second name instead. In Scotland, and among families from the north of Ireland, a common pattern named the first son after his father’s father and the first daughter after her mother’s mother. This check only looks for sons named after their father’s father and daughters named after their father’s mother, and only where that grandparent’s first name is recorded, so it misses the other customs, and the real share of children named for a grandparent was higher.

                      Cousins who married each other

                      Two people are first cousins if they share a grandparent, and second cousins if they share a great-grandparent. “Once removed” means one of them is a generation further down the family. In small farming communities, marrying a distant cousin was common, and couples didn’t always know they were related. Close links, such as an uncle marrying his niece, are much more likely to be mistakes in the tree, and they are marked that way. From the year 1215 the Church forbade marriage between people as closely related as third cousins, although wealthy families often paid for special permission.

                        What this can’t tell you

                        These are only the parents and couples who became your ancestors, not a fair sample of everyone alive at the time. Children who died young, and couples whose children didn’t survive, never appear in a family tree like this one. A marriage between relatives can only be spotted when both partners’ families are recorded, so many are missed.

                        What you inherited, in DNA

                        A family tree records who your ancestors were on paper. Your DNA is what you actually inherited from them. The two aren’t the same thing.

                        You have 23 pairs of chromosomes, the long strands your DNA is packed into. In each pair, one came from your mother and one from your father. When a parent passes a chromosome on, it isn’t passed on whole: the copy that parent got from their own mother and the copy from their own father are cut into pieces and spliced together into a new mix. So in every generation, what you receive from any one ancestor is halved on average, and it arrives in fewer and smaller pieces.

                        Go back far enough and an ancestor’s share becomes smaller than a single piece. From then on, most likely none of their DNA reached you at all, even though they are truly your ancestor.

                        The chance that at least one piece of DNA reached you from a single ancestor, by how many generations back they lived. These chances come from a standard scientific model, not from anyone’s DNA test.

                        You can see this in the circle at the top of the page: tick “Fade the ancestors who probably passed you no DNA”. Your close family stays solid, and the long lines reaching back into the Middle Ages almost disappear.

                        Two kinds of DNA that follow a single line

                        Two small parts of your DNA aren’t mixed from both parents, so they can follow one family line a very long way.

                        Mitochondrial DNA sits outside the chromosomes. Everyone gets it from their mother, but only daughters pass it on to their children. So yours came down to you along your mother’s mother’s line, unchanged or almost unchanged over many generations.

                        The Y chromosome passes only from father to son. It follows the father’s father’s line, which for you is the Boyle line. You didn’t inherit a Y chromosome yourself, but your father carries it, and so does any man descended from James Boyles through sons alone.

                            What a DNA test could and couldn’t tell you

                            • The DNA tests sold by companies such as AncestryDNA and 23andMe compare your DNA with other customers’. They reliably find second cousins, most third cousins, and about half of fourth cousins.
                            • That range suits the biggest gap in your tree. Nobody knows who Thomas and Gladys Thompson’s parents were. People descended from their brothers and sisters would be about your third cousins, close enough for a test to find, and matches like that could point to the Thompson family and to Gladys’s maiden name.
                            • On your father’s side, the Boyle line stops at James Boyles, born in 1819. Descendants of his brothers and sisters would be about your fifth cousins, whom these tests find much less reliably. A Y-DNA test, which only men can take, follows that father-to-son line and could reach further back.
                            • A test can’t confirm a connection to a medieval king. The pieces of DNA from someone that far back are too few and too small to trace, and nearly everyone with European roots descends from those same people anyway.
                            • The “ethnicity” percentages these companies show compare you with people living in different regions today. They are estimates, and they can’t tell you which of your ancestors lived where.

                            What this can’t tell you

                            The model uses average rates, and real families vary a great deal. It only counts the ancestors recorded in the tree, but your DNA also came from the many ancestors nobody wrote down. No one’s DNA was tested for this page.

                            Who was alive when

                            Choose one of the moments in history below, or drag the slider to any year, to see how many of your recorded ancestors were alive then, which side of your family they were on, and who was the oldest and youngest.

                            What this can’t tell you

                            Only ancestors with both a birth year and a death year recorded are counted. Before about 1500 most of those years are estimates, so the counts for the Middle Ages give the general picture rather than an exact number. Anyone shown as over 100 years old in those centuries almost certainly has a guessed date.

                            Crossing the ocean

                            At some point, every branch of your family that began in Europe made the journey across the Atlantic to North America. The records used here capture only a few of those journeys, because so few of your ancestors have both a birthplace and a deathplace written down.

                            A crossing told in a biography

                              During the American Revolution

                              From 1775 to 1783 the thirteen American colonies fought Britain for their independence. Colonists who stayed loyal to the British king were called Loyalists. When Britain lost the war, many Loyalists lost their homes and land, and tens of thousands moved north to what is now Canada, where the British government gave them land to start again. Your tree has an ancestor recorded on each side.

                                What this can’t tell you

                                Very few of your ancestors have places recorded at all, so most crossings leave no trace in these sources. Ship passenger lists, naturalization papers, and Norwegian and German emigration records weren’t searched for this page. WikiTree’s biography of Zacharias Hahn gives his birth year as 1828 in one place and about 1728 in another; 1728 is the one that fits his life. The letter quoted for John Lusk was written in 1860, more than a hundred years after the move it describes, by a granddaughter who was then 84.

                                Descended from kings? Gateway ancestors, and why so many people are

                                Far back in your tree are kings, queens, counts and lords. That can seem surprising. This section explains how an ordinary family tree connects to royalty, and why nearly everyone with European roots turns out to have royal ancestors.

                                What a gateway ancestor is

                                Family historians use the phrase “gateway ancestor” for the person through whom a family’s tree connects to royal or noble families. Below the gateway ancestor are ordinary farmers, tradespeople and immigrants; above, the tree opens out into titled families. In American family history the phrase usually means an immigrant to the American colonies whose descent from European nobility has been researched and published.

                                The gateway in your tree

                                This page looks for the one ancestor through whom nearly all of your noble lines pass. A person counts as noble here when their name, as written in the tree, includes a title or a noble word, such as King, Count, Jarl (a Norse nobleman) or “von”. That is a reading of the names, not a check of the records behind them.

                                Why nearly everyone descends from royalty

                                There weren’t enough people to fill the tree

                                You have 2 parents, 4 grandparents and 8 great-grandparents, and the number doubles with every generation. Thirty generations back, that makes more than a billion places in your family tree, which is more people than were alive in the whole world at the time. That only works if the same people fill many places. Over the centuries your ancestors married distant cousins again and again, so the same individuals turn up on many branches. You can see examples below, in “One person, many times over”.

                                Scientists who study this have shown that if you go back far enough, everyone alive at that time either has no living descendants at all or is an ancestor of everyone alive today in that part of the world. For Europe, that point is thought to be roughly a thousand years ago. So nearly anyone with European roots descends from almost everyone in Europe back then whose family line has continued, and that includes the kings. Two historians of royal families put it memorably: most people in Western Europe are “equally likely to be descended from the man who groomed his charger”, meaning his horse, as from William the Conqueror.

                                Nobles were the people who got written down

                                In your tree, % of the people born before 1300 have a title or noble name, compared with % of those born from 1700 on. That isn’t because your ancestors were once mostly nobles. In the Middle Ages, ordinary people were rarely written down by name. The records that survive, such as land grants, histories of kings and disputes over inheritance, were about the few families who owned land. So a family line that reaches back to the 1100s almost has to pass through those recorded families.

                                The share of people in your tree with a title or noble name, by the century they were born in.

                                Noble families had many children, and most of their descendants weren’t noble

                                Wealthy families were more likely to raise their children to adulthood, but usually only the eldest son inherited the title and the land. Younger sons and daughters often married into ordinary families, and within a few generations their descendants were farmers and tradespeople who had no idea of their noble ancestry.

                                Some royal family trees were copied, and some were invented

                                Having royal ancestors has long been a mark of status, so people have sometimes claimed it without good evidence, and old published family trees were copied from one book to the next. Online trees copy each other in the same way. Your tree shows the signs: % of the birth years before 1200 are round numbers ending in 0 or 5. Many of the stories about early Norwegian kings, such as Harald Fairhair, come from sagas, long story-histories that were written down about three hundred years after those kings lived.

                                Descent on paper isn’t the same as DNA

                                As the DNA section explains, ancestors from more than about ten generations ago often left no DNA in you at all. Harald Fairhair appears in your tree times, but all of those together count for about as much as one ancestor generations back, which is far enough that probably none of his DNA reached you.

                                So the honest answer has two parts. You almost certainly do descend from medieval royalty, just as nearly everyone with European roots does. What your tree can’t reliably tell you is which kings, and through which lines, because those very old links are the ones most often guessed, copied or invented.

                                Sources: J. T. Chang, “Recent common ancestors of all present-day individuals” (1999); D. Rohde, S. Olson and J. T. Chang, “Modelling the recent common ancestry of all living humans”, Nature (2004); P. Ralph and G. Coop, “The geography of recent genetic ancestry across Europe” (2013); J. Louda and M. Maclagan, “Lines of Succession” (1981); G. B. Roberts, “The Royal Descents of 600 Immigrants” (2004); G. Clark, “A Farewell to Alms” (2007).

                                One person, many times over

                                Because the same people fill many places in a family tree, one ancestor can be reached by many different routes. Imagine a couple with two children who each started a family. If, generations later, a descendant of one child married a descendant of the other, their children could trace back to that couple along two separate routes. Over centuries of distant cousins marrying, those routes multiply into the thousands.

                                  How long they lived

                                  In this chart every life is drawn as one thin slanted line. It starts along the bottom in the year the person was born, climbs as they grow older, and stops at the age they died. Where many lines crowd together, many of your ancestors were alive at the same time.

                                  • A life on your father’s side

                                  • A life on both sides of your family
                                  • One example life, highlighted
                                  • Short flat lines: the typical age at death for people born in one century, one set for each side of your family, in that side’s colour. Each label sits just above or below its own line.

                                  How to read this chart

                                  • The slanted lines. Each one is a single person’s life. It starts on the bottom edge at the year they were born and rises one step of age for every year they lived. Where it stops, the scale along the bottom gives the year they died, and the scale up the side gives their age at the time.
                                  • The short flat lines. Each one stands for everyone born in one century, and its label names that century and gives the age. Its height is their typical age at death: half of the people born in that century died younger than that, and half died older.
                                  • Why each flat line sits to the right of its century. A flat line is drawn over the years when those people died, not the years when they were born. People born in the 1600s mostly died in the later 1600s and in the 1700s, so the line labelled “1600s” is drawn above those later years.
                                  • What to look for. Read the flat lines from left to right. The higher they climb, the longer your ancestors typically lived.

                                  This isn’t life expectancy. In the past, many children died very young, but a child who died young never had children, so they never appear in anyone’s family tree as an ancestor. Everyone drawn here lived at least long enough to become a parent, which is why the typical age at death looks high.

                                  The years somebody guessed

                                  When a birth year is copied from a real record, such as a church’s register of baptisms, its last digit could be anything from 0 to 9, and each digit turns up about equally often. When somebody estimates a year, they tend to choose a round number ending in 0 or 5. So counting last digits shows how much of each period of your tree comes from records, and how much was filled in by guesswork.

                                  How the share of round years changes over time

                                  Each point is one fifty-year stretch of birth years on one side of your family. The line through it shows the range the number of people allows: with few people, the share is less certain. The dashed line marks 20%, the share you would expect if every year came from a record.

                                  Where the tree may be wrong

                                  A shared online tree goes wrong in some predictable ways. Two different people with the same name get merged into one. An old published family tree gets copied in whole, mistakes included. A missing date is filled in with an estimate. Or someone picks one possible parent when the records allow several. Comparing the tree with other sources shows where to look more closely.

                                  Where WikiTree names different parents

                                  WikiTree is another shared family tree. For these ancestors it has someone with the same name and dates, but different parents. Either it is a different person, or the two trees disagree. Only the original records can settle it.

                                  Your ancestorParents in FamilySearchParents in WikiTree

                                  Dates that don’t agree

                                    Names that don’t match their fathers

                                      Records that could settle these questions

                                      • Norwegian probate records were written when someone died, to divide what they owned among their heirs. They name the heirs and say how each was related, which makes them some of the best evidence of who was whose child.
                                      • Norwegian censuses list people farm by farm. The ones from 1664–66 and 1701 name men and boys, and the ones from 1801 and 1865 name everyone. These, along with church registers of baptisms, marriages and burials, can be searched for free at Digitalarkivet, the website of Norway’s national archives.
                                      • German church books recorded baptisms, marriages and burials parish by parish, in many places from the 1500s or 1600s on. The books for Cleebronn, Kleingartach and Echterdingen, villages in Württemberg, could confirm the Straile, Fritzle and Walderich families. Many Protestant church books from Württemberg can be read online through Archion, a paid website set up by Germany’s Protestant churches.
                                      • Records in Minnesota, Wisconsin, North Dakota, Pennsylvania and Ohio, where the Hone, Leininger, Wigness, Boyle, Parker and Straley families lived, such as land records, wills, state censuses and county histories.
                                      • United States censuses list every member of each household by name from 1850 to 1950, though most of the 1890 census was lost in a fire. They could trace Thomas and Gladys Thompson from place to place, and might reveal who Gladys’s parents were. They also give where each person was born, which might point to where James Boyles, born in 1819, came from.

                                      What this can’t tell you

                                      A disagreement doesn’t prove that FamilySearch is wrong. WikiTree and Wikipedia make mistakes too, and Wikipedia’s dates for medieval people are often estimates of their own. The name check is rough: it knows common spellings such as Jon, Johannes and Jan, but not every local variation, and some children took a stepfather’s name.

                                      How this page was made

                                      A family tree records who is written down as whose child, not what DNA would show. And because anyone can edit the shared tree, this page is a picture of it as it stood in September 2026, not a final word about your family.
